questions.stem: A 47 year old woman with spina bifida is having a urinary catheter inserted on the ward by a nurse wearing latex gloves. Within 10 minutes she develops widespread urticaria, wheeze and swollen lips. Her pulse rate is 136 bpm, BP 78/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A sudden allergic reaction to latex with breathing and circulation compromise is anaphylaxis; patients with spina bifida have high rates of latex allergy.

steps.x: A latex trigger with urticaria, wheeze and hypotension.

elim: Urticaria alone does not cause hypotension and hypoxia.
Develops over hours with fever, not minutes after latex contact with urticaria.
Does not cause urticaria and lip swelling within minutes.
Causes bradycardia and pallor without urticaria or wheeze.

steps.x: B: Anaphylaxis. Allergic reaction plus A, B or C compromise = anaphylaxis; latex is a classic trigger.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man takes his first dose of oral amoxicillin for a chest infection. Twenty minutes later he has crampy abdominal pain, vomits twice and feels faint. He has hives on his trunk and a hoarse voice. His temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 128 bpm, BP 84/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Vomiting, abdominal pain, hoarse voice, urticaria and hypotension minutes after a penicillin is anaphylaxis; gut symptoms are a recognised feature.

steps.x: Multi-system reaction minutes after a penicillin.

elim: Does not cause hives, a hoarse voice and hypotension within minutes.
A delayed side effect, not acute shock.
Right upper quadrant pain without urticaria or hypotension.
Would not explain hives and hoarseness within minutes of a dose.

steps.x: C: Anaphylaxis. GI symptoms plus urticaria and shock after a trigger = anaphylaxis.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman with peanut allergy eats a satay sauce. Within 10 minutes her tongue and lips swell, her voice becomes muffled and she has a high-pitched noise on breathing in. Her pulse rate is 124 bpm, BP 98/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most immediate life-threatening complication?
questions.e: The main complication of anaphylaxis is airway obstruction from mucosal oedema of the upper airway, shown here by tongue swelling, a muffled voice and stridor.

steps.x: Upper airway swelling with stridor.

elim: Can follow prolonged shock but is not the immediate threat.
Occurs hours later; the airway is the threat now.
Rare; not the main complication.
Not caused by anaphylaxis.

steps.x: B: Airway obstruction. Anaphylaxis: the main complication is airway obstruction.

questions.stem: A 6 year old boy with egg allergy eats a cake at a party. Within minutes he is in severe respiratory distress with swollen lips. His chest moves in as his abdomen moves out with each breath. His pulse rate is 150 bpm, respiratory rate 40 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. He has angioedema of the face.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on auscultation of his airway and chest?
o: Bronchial breathing at the right base
Coarse crackles that clear on coughing
questions.e: Anaphylaxis causes paradoxical see-saw breathing with inspiratory stridor (upper airway oedema) and expiratory wheeze (bronchospasm); children present with sudden respiratory distress, lip swelling and stridor.

clues: chest moves in as his abdomen moves out
steps.x: See-saw breathing with angioedema after a food trigger.

elim: Suggests consolidation, not an allergic airway.
Suggests secretions, as in bronchitis.
Suggests pulmonary oedema or fibrosis.
Possible in near-fatal asthma but stridor is expected with this angioedema.

steps.x: D: Inspiratory stridor with expiratory wheeze. Anaphylaxis: inspiratory stridor plus expiratory wheeze, see-saw breathing.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman collapses 5 minutes after an intramuscular vaccine at a travel clinic. She has widespread hives, wheeze and swollen lips. Her pulse rate is 140 bpm, BP 76/42 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air. Her skin is flushed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Collapse with tachycardia, hypotension, urticaria, angioedema and wheeze minutes after an injection is anaphylaxis; vasovagal syncope causes bradycardia and pallor without skin features.

clues: widespread hives, wheeze and swollen lips
steps.x: Tachycardia and skin features rather than bradycardia and pallor.

elim: Does not cause hypotension, wheeze and urticaria.
Causes sweating and confusion, not urticaria and wheeze.
No tonic-clonic activity; hives and wheeze point to allergy.
Causes bradycardia and pallor with rapid recovery, not tachycardia and urticaria.

steps.x: A: Anaphylaxis. Collapse with urticaria and tachycardia = anaphylaxis, not a faint.

questions.stem: A 39 year old man develops widespread hives and itchy eyes 10 minutes after a prawn curry. He then feels dizzy. On arrival his lips are not swollen and he has no wheeze or stridor. His pulse rate is 128 bpm, BP 82/46 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. His capillary refill time is 4 seconds.
questions.q: Which feature most indicates that this is anaphylaxis rather than a simple allergic reaction?
questions.e: Anaphylaxis is diagnosed by airway, breathing or circulation compromise in the context of a sudden allergic reaction; hypotension with poor perfusion is circulatory compromise even without airway signs.

steps.x: No airway or breathing problem, but circulation is compromised.

elim: Common in simple allergic reactions.
Simple reactions also start quickly.
Triggers are shared with simple reactions.
Urticaria alone is a simple allergic reaction.

steps.x: A: Hypotension. Any A, B or C compromise turns an allergic reaction into anaphylaxis.

questions.stem: A 3 year old girl at nursery suddenly develops noisy breathing and difficulty breathing 5 minutes after a snack containing sesame. She was well beforehand with no cough or fever. Her lips and tongue are swollen. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 160 bpm, respiratory rate 48 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90% breathing air. She has inspiratory stridor.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: In children anaphylaxis presents with sudden respiratory distress, lip and tongue swelling, inspiratory stridor and angioedema after a trigger; croup and epiglottitis have infective prodromes.

clues: 5 minutes after a snack containing sesame
Her lips and tongue are swollen
steps.x: Sudden stridor with angioedema after a food, afebrile.

elim: Infants under 1 with coryza, crackles and wheeze over days.
Barking cough and coryza over a day or two, without lip swelling.
High fever, drooling and toxic appearance, without lip swelling.
Sudden choking can cause stridor, but not lip and tongue swelling.

steps.x: A: Anaphylaxis. Child with sudden stridor and lip swelling after a food = anaphylaxis.

questions.stem: A 72 year old beekeeper is stung several times on his hands. Fifteen minutes later his wife finds him confused and short of breath. His temperature is 36.4°C, pulse rate 132 bpm, BP 74/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88% breathing air. His skin is mottled and his limbs are cool. He has generalised urticaria.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Confusion, hypoxia and poor perfusion with urticaria after insect stings is anaphylaxis with circulatory compromise.

steps.x: Insect stings, then confusion, hypoxia and poor perfusion with urticaria.

elim: Does not explain urticaria after stings.
Does not cause urticaria and hypotension.
Confined to the sting site, without shock.
Would not cause urticaria, hypoxia and shock.

steps.x: A: Anaphylaxis with shock. Confusion and poor perfusion after a trigger can be anaphylaxis.

questions.stem: A 15 year old girl is treated in the emergency department for anaphylaxis to peanuts. She responds to one dose of IM adrenaline and is well 1 hour later. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm, BP 112/70 mmHg and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. Her mother asks when a second reaction would most likely happen if one occurred.
questions.q: When is a biphasic reaction most likely to occur after the initial reaction?
questions.e: A biphasic reaction is a second reaction about 4 to 6 hours after the first; teenagers are particularly at risk, which is why observation is needed.

clues: when a second reaction would most likely happen
steps.x: A teenager recovering from anaphylaxis.

elim: Too late; biphasic reactions occur within hours.
Too late for a typical biphasic reaction.
This would be a continuation of the first reaction.
Too early; this is the initial phase.

steps.x: B: After 4 to 6 hours. Biphasic reaction: 4 to 6 hours later; teenagers at particular risk.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman has anaphylaxis to IV contrast. She has had two doses of IM adrenaline 5 minutes apart, high-flow oxygen and a fluid bolus. Ten minutes after the second dose she remains wheezy. Her pulse rate is 140 bpm, BP 74/40 mmHg and oxygen saturation 90% on 15 L/min oxygen. Her BP trend is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: Systolic BP
visual.caption: Systolic BP stays below 80 mmHg despite two doses of IM adrenaline.

questions.q: Which best describes her condition?
questions.e: Refractory anaphylaxis is respiratory or cardiovascular compromise persisting despite two doses of IM adrenaline; an expert should be contacted to consider an IV adrenaline infusion plus fluid.

clues: two doses of IM adrenaline 5 minutes apart
steps.x: Persisting shock and wheeze after two doses of adrenaline.

elim: A second reaction hours later, not persistent shock from the start.
Persisting shock and wheeze after contrast is ongoing anaphylaxis.
Her BP and oxygenation are not improving.
There is ongoing circulatory and respiratory compromise.

steps.x: D: Refractory anaphylaxis. Two IM doses and still compromised = refractory anaphylaxis.

questions.stem: A 16 year old boy had anaphylaxis to cashews 3 hours ago. He needed two doses of IM adrenaline and is now well. His pulse rate is 88 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. He wants to go home. His father asks which problem the team is most worried about over the next few hours.
questions.q: Which is the most likely concern over the next few hours?
questions.e: A biphasic reaction can occur 4 to 6 hours after the first, especially in teenagers and those needing two doses of adrenaline, so he should be observed for a further 6 hours.

clues: needed two doses of IM adrenaline
steps.x: Teenager, two doses needed, only 3 hours since the reaction.

elim: Adrenaline's effects wear off within minutes.
Not a complication over the next hours.
A Type IV skin reaction unrelated to this.
An immune complex reaction days to weeks later.

steps.x: B: Biphasic reaction. Teenagers and two-dose reactions: watch for a biphasic reaction.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man had anaphylaxis to IV co-amoxiclav on the ward. He received IM adrenaline and has stabilised. His pulse rate is 92 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. The ward team wants to send mast cell tryptase to support a later allergy referral.
questions.q: When should the sample ideally be taken?
o: Only if a skin prick test is positive
questions.e: Mast cell tryptase rises during and after the reaction and is ideally taken 4 to 12 hours afterwards; treatment is never delayed to take it.

steps.x: The question is about timing of the tryptase.

elim: Treatment must never be delayed for a blood test.
Tryptase will have returned to baseline.
Tryptase confirms the acute reaction regardless of skin tests.
Too late to show the rise.

steps.x: A: 4 to 12 hours after the reaction. Tryptase: ideally 4 to 12 hours after the reaction.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman is brought to the emergency department 10 minutes after eating a peanut sauce. She has stridor, widespread hives and feels faint. Her pulse rate is 136 bpm, BP 80/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90% breathing air. A junior doctor suggests sending bloods before treating.
questions.q: Which investigation is needed to establish the diagnosis before treatment?
questions.e: Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis; treatment with IM adrenaline using an ABCDE approach must not be delayed for any test.

clues: stridor, widespread hives and feels faint
steps.x: Clear airway and circulation compromise after a food trigger.

elim: Supportive only; must not delay adrenaline.
Not needed and delays treatment.
Supports the diagnosis later, but is not needed to start treatment.
Done later in allergy clinic.

steps.x: D: None; the diagnosis is clinical. Anaphylaxis: clinical diagnosis, treat immediately.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman collapsed with hypotension and wheeze at the dentist after a local anaesthetic injection. She was treated with IM adrenaline by paramedics. A blood sample taken 5 hours later is shown (see item resources). She is now well, with pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 120/78 mmHg. The allergy clinic reviews the result 3 weeks later.

visual.title: Mast cell tryptase
visual.label: 5 h: 38
visual.caption: Tryptase is well above the upper limit of 11.4 µg/L.

questions.q: Which is the most likely interpretation of the result?
questions.e: Mast cell tryptase rises after degranulation and stays raised for hours, giving retrospective biochemical confirmation of anaphylaxis.

steps.x: A raised tryptase hours after a suspected severe reaction.

elim: A single raised value after an acute event reflects the reaction, not mastocytosis.
A raised level fits the clinical event.
The value is above the reference range.
Would not raise tryptase.

steps.x: C: Mast cell degranulation, confirming anaphylaxis. Raised tryptase after the event confirms mast cell degranulation.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man is receiving an IV infusion of benzylpenicillin for cellulitis. Five minutes in he says his throat feels tight. He has widespread hives and wheeze. His pulse rate is 124 bpm, BP 88/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. The infusion is still running.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first step?
questions.e: The first step in anaphylaxis is always to remove the trigger, here by stopping the penicillin infusion, then give IM adrenaline immediately.

steps.x: The trigger is still going in.

elim: Supportive only and not the first step.
Not part of first-line treatment.
Supportive; the trigger must be removed first.
Never delays treatment.

steps.x: E: Stop the infusion. First step: remove the trigger, then IM adrenaline.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman develops itchy hives on her arms 30 minutes after eating a strawberry dessert. She has no lip or tongue swelling, voice change, wheeze or dizziness. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. A nurse has drawn up adrenaline.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Adrenaline is not needed if there are no airway, breathing or circulation problems; a simple allergic reaction is treated with an antihistamine and observation.

clues: no lip or tongue swelling, voice change, wheeze or dizziness
steps.x: Skin features only, normal observations.

elim: No airway, breathing or circulation problem, so adrenaline is not needed.
For refractory anaphylaxis only.
She is not hypotensive.
Not indicated for a simple skin reaction.

steps.x: D: Oral non-sedating antihistamine without adrenaline. No A, B or C problem: no adrenaline.

questions.stem: A 4 month old boy develops widespread hives, wheeze and floppiness 10 minutes after his first feed of cow's milk formula. His pulse rate is 190 bpm, respiratory rate 60 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 88% breathing air and capillary refill time 4 seconds. He has lip swelling.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial dose of IM adrenaline 1:1000?
questions.e: Under 6 months the IM adrenaline dose is 100 to 150 micrograms (0.1 to 0.15 ml of 1:1000).

steps.x: Anaphylaxis in an infant under 6 months.

elim: An adult cardiac arrest dose given IV, not IM in an infant.
An IV titration dose used by experts; far too low for IM use.
The dose for 6 to 12 years.
The dose for over 12s and adults.

steps.x: C: 100 to 150 micrograms. Under 6 months: 100 to 150 micrograms IM.

questions.stem: A 3 year old girl with peanut allergy eats a chocolate bar at a party. Within minutes she has stridor, swollen lips and widespread hives. Her pulse rate is 168 bpm, respiratory rate 44 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 89% breathing air and capillary refill time 4 seconds. Paramedics arrive.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate dose of IM adrenaline 1:1000?
questions.e: For children aged 6 months to 6 years the IM adrenaline dose is 150 micrograms.

steps.x: Anaphylaxis in a pre-school child.

elim: Far too high for IM use.
The dose for infants under 6 months.
The dose for 6 to 12 years.
The dose for over 12s and adults.

steps.x: C: 150 micrograms. 6 months to 6 years: 150 micrograms IM.

questions.stem: A 41 year old man has anaphylaxis to a wasp sting. He has stridor and his BP is 82/48 mmHg. His pulse rate is 134 bpm, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air. A nurse prepares adrenaline 500 micrograms (0.5 ml of 1:1000) and asks where to give it.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate site of injection?
o: Peripheral vein as an IV bolus
questions.e: IM adrenaline is given into the middle third of the anterolateral thigh (vastus lateralis), which gives faster, more reliable absorption than subcutaneous or other IM sites.

steps.x: The dose is right; the question is the site.

elim: Absorption is less reliable than the vastus lateralis.
Slower, less reliable absorption.
IV bolus adrenaline in the conscious patient risks arrhythmia; IV is for experts only.
Subcutaneous absorption is too slow.

steps.x: A: Anterolateral thigh. IM adrenaline: middle third of the anterolateral thigh.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman on a surgical ward is due IV co-amoxiclav. A nurse new to the ward picks up the bag, and the patient in the next bed has a similar name. Her drug chart has a red wristband warning. She is well: pulse rate 76 bpm, BP 128/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate step before giving the antibiotic?
o: Check three-point identity and allergy status
Give a small test dose first
questions.e: Three-point patient identification and checking allergies are vital before giving any medication, preventing exposure to a known trigger such as a penicillin.

steps.x: Possible patient mix-up and a possible allergy flag.

elim: Does not prevent anaphylaxis and still exposes the patient.
No role before a drug.
Does not prevent anaphylaxis.
Used after a reaction, not before a drug.

steps.x: A: Check three-point identity and allergy status. Before any drug: three-point ID and check allergies.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman with anaphylaxis to a sesame snack has just had IM adrenaline 500 micrograms. She is lying flat with her legs raised. Her pulse rate is 138 bpm, BP 78/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. IV access has been obtained.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step while assessing her response?
o: High-flow oxygen and an IV fluid bolus
questions.e: Using an ABCDE approach, give oxygen if hypoxic, wheezy or shocked and IV fluids if hypotensive, while repeating IM adrenaline after 5 minutes if needed.

steps.x: Hypoxic and hypotensive after the first dose.

elim: She is shocked and hypoxic.
Too slow and does not treat shock.
Sitting up a hypotensive patient can worsen shock.
Reassess continuously; a repeat dose is due at 5 minutes if needed.

steps.x: C: High-flow oxygen and an IV fluid bolus. ABCDE: oxygen for hypoxia, IV fluid for shock.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man with anaphylaxis to a bee sting had IM adrenaline 500 micrograms 5 minutes ago. He still has stridor and wheeze. His pulse rate is 130 bpm, BP 84/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% on high-flow oxygen. A fluid bolus is running.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Repeat IM adrenaline and call for senior support
Start an IV adrenaline infusion on the ward
questions.e: If there is no improvement 5 minutes after the first dose, IM adrenaline is repeated with urgent senior or resuscitation team support.

steps.x: No response 5 minutes after one dose.

elim: Steroids do not act quickly and are not first line.
Too slow.
An infusion is for refractory anaphylaxis after two IM doses, with expert help.
Adrenaline is repeated after 5 minutes if needed.

steps.x: C: Repeat IM adrenaline and call for senior support. Repeat IM adrenaline at 5 minutes and get senior help.

questions.stem: A 23 year old woman with anaphylaxis to shellfish has had one dose of IM adrenaline, oxygen and IV fluid. Her lip swelling and hives are settling and her BP has risen to 116/70 mmHg. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm and oxygen saturation 95% on oxygen. She still has a mild expiratory wheeze.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional treatment?
questions.e: Once adrenaline has been given, supportive measures include antihistamines and nebulised bronchodilators if wheezy.

clues: still has a mild expiratory wheeze
steps.x: Circulation recovered; residual wheeze only.

elim: Not needed; she has responded.
No infection.
Wrong dose, and her circulation has recovered.
Her BP has recovered.

steps.x: B: Nebulised salbutamol. Supportive care: nebulised bronchodilator for wheeze, antihistamine for itch.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man was treated for anaphylaxis to peanuts. He needed one dose of IM adrenaline and has been observed for 6 hours with no further symptoms. His pulse rate is 76 bpm, BP 124/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. He is ready for discharge and has an allergy clinic referral.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional discharge plan?
o: Regular cetirizine instead of an auto-injector
Two adrenaline auto-injectors with training and avoidance advice
questions.e: On discharge, patients receive two adrenaline auto-injectors with training, trigger avoidance advice and allergy clinic referral.

clues: observed for 6 hours with no further symptoms
steps.x: Safe for discharge after observation.

elim: No role in preventing anaphylaxis.
He needs auto-injectors and avoidance advice.
Two are prescribed in case a second dose is needed.
Antihistamines do not treat anaphylaxis.

steps.x: E: Two adrenaline auto-injectors with training and avoidance advice. Discharge: two auto-injectors, training, avoidance, allergy clinic.

questions.stem: A 14 year old girl had anaphylaxis to sesame 1 hour ago. She needed two doses of IM adrenaline and is now symptom free. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm, BP 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. Her parents want to take her home now.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Discharge now with an allergy referral
Observe in hospital for a further 6 hours
questions.e: Discharge decisions are risk-stratified; needing two doses of adrenaline and being a teenager increase the risk of a biphasic reaction, so she should be observed for a further 6 hours and assessed by the allergy team.

clues: needed two doses of IM adrenaline
steps.x: Higher-risk features despite current recovery.

elim: Two doses were needed and she is a teenager; observation is needed.
She needs observation and auto-injectors.
She has responded and is symptom free.
She is stable; observation on a ward is enough.

steps.x: C: Observe in hospital for a further 6 hours. Two doses or a teenager: observe for a further 6 hours.

questions.stem: A 37 year old man has anaphylaxis 5 minutes after eating peanuts. He has hives, wheeze and hypotension. His pulse rate is 130 bpm, BP 80/46 mmHg and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air. Months earlier he had a mild reaction to peanuts. A student asks how the reaction is classified.
questions.q: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is this?
questions.e: Anaphylaxis is a severe systemic Type I IgE-mediated reaction: allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells and basophils, releasing histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes and prostaglandins.

clues: Months earlier he had a mild reaction to peanuts
steps.x: Immediate reaction after prior sensitisation.

elim: Antibody against cell-surface antigens, as in transfusion reactions.
Immune complex deposition, as in serum sickness.
Delayed T-cell reaction over days, as in contact dermatitis.
Stimulating autoantibodies, as in Graves' disease.

steps.x: A: Type I. Anaphylaxis = Type I, IgE-mediated.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman develops anaphylaxis after IV gelatin. She has widespread urticaria, facial angioedema and wheeze. Her pulse rate is 140 bpm, BP 72/38 mmHg and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air. Her jugular venous pressure is not visible. A student asks why her BP has fallen.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her hypotension?
questions.e: Mast cell mediators cause widespread vasodilation and increased vascular permeability, shifting fluid out of vessels and causing hypotension, angioedema and urticaria; bronchospasm causes the wheeze.

clues: jugular venous pressure is not visible
steps.x: Low BP, empty veins and tissue swelling.

elim: Causes wheeze, not hypotension.
She has not vomited; the onset is too fast.
No evidence; the cause is mediator release.
Would not cause urticaria and angioedema.

steps.x: E: Vasodilation and increased vascular permeability. Shock in anaphylaxis: vasodilation plus leaky capillaries.

questions.stem: A 25 year old woman has anaphylaxis with widespread wheeze after a wasp sting. Within minutes of IM adrenaline her wheeze settles, her peak flow improves and her pulse rate rises from 118 to 130 bpm. Her BP is 108/66 mmHg and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. A student asks how adrenaline relieved the wheeze.
questions.q: Which receptor action is mainly responsible for the relief of wheeze?
questions.e: Adrenaline acts on beta-2 receptors to cause bronchodilation and reduce further mediator release, beta-1 to increase heart rate and contractility, and alpha-1 to vasoconstrict.

clues: pulse rate rises from 118 to 130 bpm
steps.x: Two effects: the bronchi relax and the heart speeds up.

elim: Raises BP and reduces oedema but does not relax the bronchi.
Not the mechanism of bronchodilation.
Explains the rise in pulse, not the wheeze.
The action of ipratropium, not adrenaline.

steps.x: D: Beta-2 bronchodilation. Adrenaline: beta-2 bronchodilation, beta-1 heart, alpha-1 vessels.

questions.stem: A 17 year old boy treated for anaphylaxis to peanuts recovered fully after IM adrenaline. Five hours later, without any further exposure, he develops new hives and wheeze. His pulse rate is 118 bpm, BP 100/60 mmHg and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. A student asks why this happened.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the second reaction?
o: Second wave of mediator release from recruited inflammatory cells
questions.e: A biphasic reaction is a second wave of mediator release hours later, thought to relate to recruitment of additional inflammatory cells, without further allergen exposure.

clues: Five hours later, without any further exposure
steps.x: Recurrence hours later without re-exposure.

elim: Adrenaline wears off within minutes, not 5 hours.
A Type IV reaction takes days.
Type III reactions such as serum sickness take days to weeks.
He has had no further exposure.

steps.x: E: Second wave of mediator release from recruited inflammatory cells. Biphasic reaction: second wave of mediator release from recruited cells.
